about: Mogontia (Mainz), one port. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/mogontia.md and the spine (Design/content/spine.json), in step with places/daventre.json (the hostage Brunric). A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what could not be checked.

ports.summary: Mogontia is the old Roman city on the west bank of the Rhine where the Main comes in: a wall far too long for the people inside it, an archbishop, a mint, and a shore of long plots and jetties where Frisian shippers live. A merchant comes for wine from the hills all round and for the grain the Main boats bring down, and brings cloaks, pots and whatever the sea sells. It is the top of the river for a small boat: every mile here was hauled on a rope, and everything bought here rides home on the stream.
ports.seasons: The year turns on the vine: pruning in the cold, the vintage in the weeks after Michaelmas, new wine in the cask by Martinmas and the Frisians gone downriver with it before the ice. Saint Alban's day at midsummer fills the hill with pilgrims, mid-Lent brings the bishop's business, and the Rhine runs high from the Alps' snow in early summer, when the haul up is slowest.

history.text: About this year the bishop of Mainz becomes an archbishop: his province grows into the largest north of the Alps.
Riculf, a Frank of the Wetterau and a pupil of Alcuin, becomes archbishop. He begins a great church for Saint Alban on the hill south of the wall.
This year there was famine. In autumn the king's ditch between the Main's waters and the Danube's was given up, and at Christmas his boats came down the Main.
On 10 August Queen Fastrada died at Frankfurt and was buried at Saint Alban's. The same summer the king's council at Frankfurt made the penny heavier and set a top price on grain and bread.
About this year Riculf sent his old master Alcuin an ivory comb, and Alcuin thanked him with a riddle: a beast with two heads and sixty teeth, and not as big as an elephant.
history.source: Things That Talk, after Sorrell, 'Alcuin's comb riddle' (dossier 7); the letter is in MGH Epistolae IV (?)

history.text: The king held his assembly at Mainz before he went to Rome.
The king held his assembly at Mainz. About this year his timber bridge on the old Roman piers was begun: five hundred paces long, and ten years in the building.
history.source: chronicle_793.json: 803-mainz-803; Einhard, Life of Charles 17, 32 (tr. Turner 1880); de.wikipedia 'Rheinbrücke Karls des Großen' (begun 803, finished 813). The year it was begun is a reckoning back from the fire of 813 by Einhard's ten years (?)

history.text: About this year thirty-seven Saxon hostages, kept by bishops and counts among the Alemans, were ordered brought to Mainz at mid-Lent. On 1 December Saint Alban's basilica was consecrated.
history.source: Indiculus obsidum Saxonum Moguntiam deducendorum, MGH Capitularia I no. 115 (?), as in spine.json saxon_end; de.wikipedia 'Stift St. Alban vor Mainz'

history.text: The relics of Saint Caesarius were brought to Saint Alban's. From 9 to 11 December a fast was kept against the plague on men and cattle.
In May the king's bridge, hardly finished, burned in three hours. On 9 June a council for the mending of the church sat at Saint Alban's. On 9 August Riculf died.
history.source: Einhard, Life of Charles 32 (tr. Turner 1880); de.wikipedia 'Rheinbrücke Karls des Großen' (finished 813) (?); Annales Fuldenses 813; chronicle_793.json: 813-summer-reform-councils; de.wikipedia 'Richulf'

history.text: On Saint John's day Harald, a king of the Danes, was baptised with his wife and many of his people: at Saint Alban's, the annals of Fulda say; at the palace of Ingelheim, others say.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 826; de.wikipedia 'Otgar von Mainz'; en.wikipedia 'Harald Klak' (dossier 8)

history.text: On 20 June the emperor Louis died on an island in the Rhine by Ingelheim. In August two kings' armies lay facing each other outside Mainz.
At the sharing of the kingdom Mainz went to Louis, king of the eastern Franks.

Hrabanus, born in this city, was made archbishop and held a council at Saint Alban's. A woman called Thiota, who had foretold the end of the world for that year, was flogged; she said a priest had taught her the words for gain.
This year there was famine: a measure of wheat cost ten pieces of silver at Mainz, and Hrabanus fed more than three hundred poor every day at Winkel.
On 1 January the earth shook: the old walls split, and Saint Michael's oratory at the west end of Saint Alban's fell.
This year there was famine, and then locusts a thumb long that lay like snow and stripped a hundred iugera near Mainz in an hour.

On 30 December, before cockcrow, the earth shook: pots knocked together and broke, as the potters said. That winter the Northmen burned Colonia and Bonn, and their clergy fled to Mainz with treasures and the bodies of saints.
The Northmen having burned as far as Koblenz, the wall of Mainz began to be mended and a ditch was dug outside it.
The Northmen came up the Rhine; Archbishop Liutbert met them with a few men, killed many and took back the plunder. They never reached Mainz.
In March, after mid-Lent, the best part of the city burned, where the Frisians lived. From May to July the Rhine flooded from its source to the sea.
On 26 June Archbishop Sunderold was killed fighting the Northmen on the Geul. Hatto followed him, and in his time the river wall was rebuilt nearer the water.
Liutefred, a rich merchant of Mainz, went as King Otto's envoy to the Greek emperor: he left Venice on 25 August and reached Constantinople on 17 September.
history.source: Liudprand, Antapodosis VI.4 (tr. F. A. Wright 1930)

history.text: From July to September King Otto besieged his son Liudolf and Conrad the Red in Mainz.
A traveller from Tortosa, Ibrahim son of Yaqub, saw at Mainz silver struck at Samarkand fifty years before, and pepper, ginger, cloves, spikenard, costus and galangal, so far in the west.
history.source: G. Jacob, Ein arabischer Berichterstatter aus dem 10. Jahrhundert (1896), pp. 37-38; chronicle_793.json: 965-ibrahim-hedeby

history.text: Willigis, of free but not noble birth, became archbishop: chancellor and later regent of the kingdom, and the first archbishop in it to put his own head on a coin.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Willigis'; Landesmuseum Mainz, Aurea Magontia: 'Archbishop Willigis'

history.text: On 7 June Willigis crowned Henry king at Mainz.
On the day it was to be consecrated, 29 or 30 August, Willigis's new cathedral burned.
King Henry drove the Jews out of Mainz; they were back within a few years (?).
On 10 November the rebuilt cathedral was consecrated.
In October Pope Leo and the emperor Henry held a synod of forty bishops at Mainz against the buying of church offices and the marriage of priests.

eras.text: Riculf's city. A Roman wall round more gardens than houses, the Frisians' plots and jetties on the shore, stone going up the hill for Saint Alban's, the king at Ingelheim or Frankfurt and never far. From about 803 the king's carpenters are laying a timber bridge on the old piers; in May 813, hardly finished, it burns.

The emperor Louis's years. The piers stand bare again and the ferry keeps its trade. Otgar is archbishop from 826, the year a Danish king is baptised; grain men boat pilgrims down the Main to Einhard's new saints. In 840 two armies face each other outside the wall.

The eastern kingdom's first city. Hrabanus, born here, feeds the hungry in 850; councils sit at Saint Alban's; the earth shakes again and again and the old wall splits. Dorestad dies downriver and the Frisians who come up are fewer and richer.

The frightened years. Colonia's clergy and their saints lodge here; the wall is mended and a ditch dug; in 886 the Frisians' shore burns and the Rhine floods. Under Hatto the river wall moves forward to the water and the bishop becomes lord of the city.

The Ottonian kings' city. Rich merchants of the town go as far as the Greek emperor; Jewish traders from Italy and the south settle; a king besieges his own son here in 953; by 965 Samarkand silver and Indian spice lie on a stall.

Willigis's city, now called golden. He is the king's chancellor, strikes coin with his own head, and builds a cathedral east of Saint Martin's with bronze doors. It burns on its consecration day in 1009 and he begins again.

The crowning city. Kings are made here in 1002 and 1024; the cathedral is consecrated at last in 1036; a pope sits in synod in 1049. The Jews have a school known as far as Spain and a graveyard outside the wall.

sites.name: The Frisians' shore
sites.see: In front, a gravel bank with river boats nosed onto it and short plank jetties running out from long narrow plots. Behind, timber houses gable-on to the water, and behind them the grey Roman wall, taller than any roof. Tow ropes dry on rails; it smells of wet hemp, wine lees and pitch, and Frisian is spoken louder than Frankish.
sites.source: Landesmuseum Mainz, Aurea Magontia, 'From near and far': long plots from the wall to the river with jetties, Frisian traders settled there; Annales Fuldenses 886. Certain in 886, likely earlier, undated for 793 (dossier 8)

sites.name: The river gate
sites.see: A Roman gate arch in the wall above the shore, its stone worn hollow by cart wheels, with a lean-to of planks against it where the bishop's man sits with a tally stick. Through the arch, a strip of street and then cabbages. Carts of casks wait in a line; a mule complains.
sites.source: The Roman wall: de.wikipedia 'Mainzer Stadtmauer'. No Mainz tariff is known; only old and just tolls are lawful (capitulary of 805; Design/economy_and_trade.md). The gate and the toll man's seat are a guess (?)

sites.name: The market inside the gate
sites.see: A widening of the old street between the wall and the bishop's church: casks on their sides, sacks of Main wheat, stacked pots from downriver, a Frisian with cloaks over his arm. Roman paving shows through the mud. Hens, a hand-bell, and the new wine sharp in the air after Michaelmas.
sites.source: The market's site is unknown (dossier 8): placed by the river gate as a guess. Goods: dossier 4 (wine, Main grain, Badorf and Mayen pots, Frisian cloaks)

sites.name: The wine cellars under the wall
sites.see: Low stone vaults dug into the foot of the wall, older than anyone's grandfather, with casks two deep on oak rails and a boy asleep on the top row. A tallow lamp, a chalk tally on the door post. Cold, and the smell of a hundred vintages in the stone.
sites.source: Wine from the country round Mainz (Jacob 1896, for 965; Design/economy_and_trade.md: wine from south of Mainz in Dorestad's casks). Roman vaults reused as cellars are a guess (?)

sites.name: The mint by Saint Martin's
sites.see: A stone room with one barred window, a charcoal hearth, an oak block with the lower die set in it and a man holding the upper die while another swings. A scale hangs from a beam over a cloth. The ring of the hammer comes out into the street a beat late.
sites.source: A penny of Charles's early type (771-794), CARO/LVS, 1.32 g, struck at Mainz: Münzkabinett Berlin, object 18245022. Merovingian moneyers of Mainz: Landesmuseum Mainz, 'Living on the Rhine'. Where the mint stood is a guess

sites.name: Saint Martin's, the bishop's church
sites.see: An old stone church among lower roofs, patched with Roman brick, its door open on a dark nave with one lamp at the far end. Clerks cross the yard with wax tablets. A bell, slow chant at the hours, and beeswax over the smell of the street.
sites.source: de.wikipedia 'St. Johannis (Mainz)': the old cathedral, rebuilt by Hatto about 900; what stood in 793 is unknown (dossier 2), so the look is a guess. From about 1000 Willigis's cathedral rises east of it ('Mainzer Dom')

sites.name: The bishop's hall
sites.see: A long timber hall on stone footings beside the church, benches down both walls, a table at the end covered with tablets, tally sticks and one precious ink-horn. Petitioners wait by the door with their caps in their hands. Rush-smoke, wet wool, and a clerk's voice reading a list.
sites.source: Invented as a building; the archbishop's court and the hostages brought to Mainz at mid-Lent are from the Indiculus obsidum (MGH Capitularia I no. 115) (?). By about 900 the archbishop is lord of the city (regionalgeschichte.net)

sites.name: Saint Alban's on the hill
sites.see: South of the wall the road climbs between old graves to a building yard: lime pits, ox-carts of stone, and the walls of a great three-aisled church rising round a small old one. From 805 it stands whole, fifty paces long. Below, the whole bend of the river and the mouth of the Main. Mason's hammers, then, later, a school reciting.
sites.source: de.wikipedia 'Stift St. Alban vor Mainz': a graveyard since Roman times, Riculf's basilica about 75 m long consecrated 1 December 805, graves of Fastrada (794) and the archbishops; Einhard, Translation (tr. Wendell 1926): 'both a church and a very celebrated monastery'

sites.name: Ratburg's ale-house on the shore
sites.see: A long low house on a Frisian plot, its door to the river, with a bench outside where haulers sit with their boots off and their feet in a tub. Inside, one hearth, two trestles and a tafl board scratched on a cask head. Ale, onions, wet rope, and three tongues arguing about the price of a tow.
sites.source: Invented; the shore and its people are the Landesmuseum's (From near and far). The house burns with the shore in 886 (Annales Fuldenses)

sites.name: The ferry to Kastel, under the old piers
sites.see: A flat ferry barge on a pole at the foot of a lane, and out in the stream twenty-one stone piers in a line to the far bank, each with a bush growing on top and brown water piling against it. Beyond, the low walls of the old fort at Kastel. Herons on the piers; the ferryman shouting at a horse.
sites.source: de.wikipedia 'Römerbrücke (Mainz)': 21 stone piers, about 600 m; 'Mainz-Kastel'. The crossing is by boat: the king's bridge, ten years in the building from about 803, burned in May 813 when it was hardly finished (Einhard 17, 32; de.wikipedia 'Rheinbrücke Karls des Großen'). The ferrymen are named only in modern retellings of the fire (dossier 7)

sites.name: The king's bridge
sites.see: New timber going onto the old stone, a little further each year: a roadway of oak beams from the river gate toward Kastel, five hundred paces long when it is done, pale and sharp-edged, with boats passing under between the piers. In the spring of 813 it is whole, and carts drum across it. It smells of fresh-cut oak and tar, and people come out on feast days only to walk on it.
sites.source: Einhard, Life of Charles 17 and 32 (tr. Turner 1880): five hundred paces, ten years in the building, burned in three hours in May 813. Begun about 803 and finished in 813: de.wikipedia 'Rheinbrücke Karls des Großen' (a reckoning from Einhard's ten years (?)); so the site is a building work until its last spring. Ships passed under it: Notker, Deeds of Charles I.30 (tr. Grant 1905)

sites.name: The potters' row and the pin-makers
sites.see: A lane of sheds against the inside of the wall: wheels turning, grey pots drying in rows on planks, a kiln breathing through its roof. At the end a man casts brooches in a clay mould no bigger than his hand and files them bright. Wood smoke, wet clay, and the click of pots being tried with a knuckle.
sites.source: Annales Fuldenses 881 (the potters of Mainz and their pots); Landesmuseum Mainz, 'From near and far': brooches made on the spot, sherds of Badorf and Mayen ware from the shore dig

sites.name: The smiths' yard by the south gate
sites.see: Three forges under one long roof on the road out to Saint Alban's, horses waiting to be shod, a rack of spurs and bits, and at the back a locked chest the smith does not open for strangers. A king's man leans on the gatepost most days and counts who goes in. Hot iron, hoof-parings, hammer and bellows.
sites.source: Mounted warriors with fine spurs at Mainz: Landesmuseum Mainz, 'Strategic centre'. No mail coat may leave the realm (Herstal 779) and no arms be sold to strangers (Thionville 805): spine.json swords_north. The yard is invented; nailed horseshoes are not surely attested before the 9th or 10th century, so horses waiting to be shod in 793 are a guess (?)

sites.name: The boat bank below the wall
sites.see: Downstream of the jetties the bank is all chips and trestles: a flat barge half planked, a long oak log being hollowed, a raft of Main timber tied to stakes and waiting to be broken up. Men caulk with moss and tar. Adzes knock; pitch boils in a pot.
sites.source: Design/content/ships.md (river craft at every Rhine port, built upstream; the Krefeld-Gellep barge; hauling by rope); boats lying on the shore below the wall: Landesmuseum Mainz. The yard itself is a guess

sites.name: The Drusus stone and the old theatre
sites.see: On the high ground by Saint Alban's road a round stone tower with no door, sixty feet high, older than the wall; below it a great half-bowl of broken seats grown over with elder, and graves dug into its vaults. Wind in the grass. Boys herd goats where ten thousand once sat.
sites.source: de.wikipedia 'Drususstein' (a Roman tower-tomb about 20 m high); 'Mogontiacum' (the theatre of about 10,000 seats, graves in its vaults from the 6th century)

sites.name: The spice men by the river gate
sites.see: Three stalls under one awning, kept by men in long gowns who speak Frankish with a southern lilt and write in letters of their own: small leather bags, a folding scale, a bowl of foreign silver with no king's face on it. Pepper and cloves reach the nose before the eye finds them.
sites.source: Jacob 1896 (Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, 965): dirhams of Samarkand of 301 and 302 of the Hijra, and pepper, ginger, cloves, spikenard, costus, galangal. Jewish long-distance traders at Mainz from the mid-10th century: de.wikipedia 'Jüdische Gemeinde Mainz'; Landesmuseum Mainz, 'The Jewish community'. The stalls' place is a guess

people.name: Riculf
people.trait: A courtier turned builder: quick, well read, easy with kings, and impatient with any stone that is not yet on the hill.
people.want: Stone, lime, lead and glass for Saint Alban's, and a dry boat for his letters and gifts to his old master.
people.fear: Dying before the basilica is hallowed; the king hearing bad news of Mainz from somebody else first.
people.voice: Light and fast, a schoolman's jokes, calls his friends by the names they had in class; never raises his voice.
people.looks: About fifty-five, lean, tonsured grey hair, a fine dark wool cloak over white linen, a bishop's ring, an ivory comb in a case at his belt and lime dust on his hem.
knows: what the church pays for wax, lead, lime, glass and stone
where the king is and where he will keep the next feast
the new rules on coin, measure and the price of grain
who at court will read a letter and who will lose it

ties.note: Alcuin taught him and calls him Damoetas (?); Riculf sends him a comb and gets a riddle back
his clerk, who remembers what the bishop promises
the archbishop of Colonia is the king's own chaplain; each counts the other's days at court
both men of Alcuin's school; Liudger's Saxons and Riculf's hostages are the same war
a brother bishop downriver; they exchange wax for wine and complaints for complaints
the clerk at Colonia sends the hostage rolls up when the king orders it; Riculf has never met him and knows his hand better than his own clerk's
the moneyer strikes for the king under the bishop's eye; Riculf looks in at the mint twice a year and understands a third of what he is shown
a canon at Saint Bavo's on the Scheldt copies every letter of Alcuin's that passes and once sent to ask, humbly, for the comb riddle (?)

lines.greet: You came up on the rope from Dorestat? Then you have earned a seat. What do you carry, and whose is it?
lines.greet_again: You again. A man who comes twice up this river is either honest or stubborn. I can use both.
rumour: The king's ditch between the Main and the Danube is given up. Rain filled it faster than men could dig. He came home by boat.
The queen lies on the hill now, at Saint Alban's. The king chose the place. I would like a roof over her before I die.
My old master writes from Tours that his books are too few and his teeth fewer. He wants both mended from here.
lines.trade: Lead, lime and good stone for the hill; wax always. My clerk pays by weight the same day, which is not the custom of bishops.
lines.warm: I will write three lines to Hildebold at Colonia. He is the king's chaplain. Three lines from me get you past his door-ward.
lines.saying: My master says a comb is a beast with two heads and sixty teeth. A bishop is a beast with one head and sixty petitioners.
lines.farewell: Go down easily. The river does the work that way. It is the only thing in this city that does.

people.source: de.wikipedia 'Richulf': archbishop 787-813, a Frank of the Wetterau, Alcuin's pupil, builder of Saint Alban's, died 9 August 813. His birth year is unknown (0). The comb: Things That Talk, after Sorrell. The school name Damoetas is from memory (?). His character and words are invented

people.name: Otbert
people.trait: The bishop's list-keeper: hostages, hulls, books, measures. Exact, nosy, and kinder than his lists.
people.want: Every list whole; and a copy of Bede on the reckoning of time, which the school has asked England for twice.
people.fear: A gap in a list on the day the king's envoy reads it; a book lent and never seen again.
people.voice: Counts on his fingers while he talks; answers a question by finding the right tablet.
people.looks: About thirty, small and round-shouldered, tonsured brown hair, an ink-stained grey tunic, wax tablets on a thong at his belt and a stylus behind his ear.
knows: who is on the bishop's lists and why
the king's measure and the top price of grain
which churches want which books, and who has a copy
the day and place of the hostages' counting

ties.note: writes his letters and keeps his promises for him
in 826, his last year, a new archbishop finds him still at the lists and leaves him there; Otbert counts the Danes' baptismal linen and comes up nine short
they trade copies up and down the river and each thinks the other got the better book
the York monk carries what Otbert asks England for; they have never met
wrote the Saxon's name on the list and took the trouble to spell it as the man says it
the palace clerk's tallies and his never quite agree
the clerk at Colonia sends the hostage rolls up to him when the king orders it; they write to each other in lists
Gundhart is the first name on his list of hulls and the only grain man whose measure he has never had to strike twice
the book-keeper at Saint Bavo's and he have each other's leaf-counts by way of Traiectum; each is sure the other is hiding a book
has never seen her: a Saxon woman in the king's kitchen at the Ruhr mouth whose count of the hostage bands, sent up by a boatman, agreed with his roll where the steward's did not

lines.greet: Name, home port, cargo. No, I am not the toll. I like to know. Mind the wax.
lines.greet_again: I have you written down, under the grain men. You were honest last time. I made a mark.
rumour: The king has ordered one measure for grain everywhere. The new one stands in this hall. Bring yours and learn how much you have been cheating.
Traiectum's schoolmaster wants our Bede on the reckoning of time. I want his Aldhelm. Neither of us trusts the river with it.
lines.hostages: Thirty-seven names and their keepers, all to stand in this hall at mid-Lent. I am to count them twice. Only hostages get counted twice.
lines.warm: I can put a name before the bishop or under forty others. Yours goes on top. Do not make me regret my handwriting.
lines.saying: What is not written did not happen. What is written twice happened to two people.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and tell me next time what the toll took at Colonia. I keep a list.

people.source: invented (Ot- + -bert). The lists are real kinds: the Indiculus obsidum of about 805 (?), with its thirty-seven hostages (how many keepers it names was not checked, so he gives no number), the public modius of Frankfurt 794; Lul of Mainz wrote to Wearmouth-Jarrow for Bede's works (spine.json book_road) (?)

people.name: Folcbald
people.trait: A Frisian wine shipper thirty years on this shore: dry, patient, buys at the vintage and sells when others are thirsty.
people.want: A partner downriver he can trust with forty casks, so that he need never haul a rope again.
people.fear: A bad vintage in a year he has promised wine; Thiadbod's house buying the plots either side of his.
people.voice: Says the price last and says it once; makes his jokes with a straight face and waits.
people.looks: About forty, spare and weathered, fair hair gone thin, a short blue Frisian cloak with a bronze pin, a cellar key on a thong and a wooden tasting cup at his belt.
knows: what the growers ask at the vintage and what the same cask fetches at Dorestad
which abbey's cellarer is short this year
the haul upriver: the gorge, Saint Goar's cell, where to hire a gang
who on the shore is buying, and with whose silver

ties.note: sells him wine and will not sell him land; Thiadbod calls him cousin and is not one
her late husband stood surety for his first cellar; he sends her a cask each Martinmas
the palace cellarer paid ahead for a vintage that failed; Folcbald still owes six casks
his tenant on the next plot; she pays her rent in news
the Witla skipper takes his wine on over the sea to the English
the potter's widow fills her jars with his wine for the north; each says the other's goods make their own worth carrying
the Main men and the Frisians share one shore and one ale-house, and agree about neither
Liutwin's house at Colonia buys from him when its own growers are short and has three times offered for the cask he does not sell
the cellarer of Saint Peter's on the Scheldt wants one cask a year for the Mass, since the vines on his own hill give vinegar; it goes round by Dorestad and is paid for in wool cloth
the monk of the salt pans at Herio keeps the leaf before his; they have never met, and send word by salt ships (?)

lines.greet: From Dorestat, by the rope? Then you know what my wine costs before it is wine: weeks of other men's backs.
lines.greet_again: You came back up. Nobody does that for pleasure. Sit. I will open the cask I do not sell.
rumour: Thiadbod's man was here before the vintage, buying on a promise. I sold him the promise's worth. He looked at the casks a long time.
The Main men say the grain upriver is thin again. When grain is thin, wine is cheap: men sell what they can spare.
lines.riddle: A monk left me a verse: born in the furnace, looks like ice, puts men on the floor. I sell what goes in it. You tell me.
lines.warm: Leave silver with me at the vintage and forty casks lie cellared for you by Martinmas, at the grower's price and my tenth.
lines.saying: The king says our cloaks are short. He bought them. A short cloak sold is longer than a long one on the shelf.
lines.farewell: Go with the stream, and stop at Saint Goar's to pray. I know of two skippers who did not. It cost one silver and one silk.

people.source: invented (Folc- + -bald). Frisian traders on the Mainz shore: Landesmuseum Mainz; Annales Fuldenses 886. The cloaks: Notker I.34. Saint Goar's due: Wandalbert, Miracula sancti Goaris (about 839). He holds the glass-cup riddle of riddles_793.json (riddle_aldhelm_80_calix_vitreus: 'a Frisian wine shipper of the Frisian quarter')

people.name: Ratburg
people.trait: Keeps the haulers' ale-house on a Frisian plot: sharp-eyed, loud, loyal to anyone who pays the score and comes back.
people.want: Her brother the ferryman kept out of trouble, and a second hearth so the Main men and the Frisians need not share one.
people.fear: The king's bridge, which will take her brother's trade when it is done; after 813, the question of who burned it.
people.voice: Frankish with Frisian curses in it; talks while she pours and stops pouring when she wants an answer.
people.looks: About thirty-five, broad and strong-armed, a linen head-cloth, sleeves rolled, a brown gown with a bone pin, a dipper in one hand and a tally stick of scores in her belt.
knows: who is in harbour, who is hiring and who left without paying
what the ferrymen see from the river by night
the price of a hauling gang this week
everything said on her benches, a day before the bishop's hall hears it

ties.note: his tenant; they have argued about the rent for fifteen years and enjoyed it
her mother's brother; he will not drink her ale and she will not use his scale
the one hauler who never broke a bench; she pours for him without asking where he is from
one alewife to another by way of the boats: the Daventre woman's question about a hostage boy reached her years ago
says the ale-house in the tower at Colonia waters the ale and salts the news; they trade both by every boat
his boatmen drink on one stick all year and he settles it at Martinmas in barley, which is why her ale is better than her manners
the ale-wife at the Ruhr mouth: three houses on one river, and a word put in at any of them is at the other two within the month

lines.greet: Rope hands. Show me. Yes, you hauled her yourself. First pot is mine to give, for any skipper with his own blisters.
lines.greet_again: Your bench is kept. A Main man sat on it at Easter and I moved him.
rumour: My brother poles the ferry to Kastel. He says the king's men are measuring the old piers again. Kings measure. Ferrymen eat.
The potters swear their kilns draw badly before a hard winter. They also swear their pots are sound. Believe one of the two.
lines.crew: Two haulers want a berth down to the sea. One is a Saxon who will not say where from. He works. I ask no more.
lines.fire: It burned in the time of three slow psalms. My brother was asleep in my loft. I will swear that before any bishop.
lines.saying: New wine by Martinmas, new quarrels by Advent.
lines.farewell: Mind the piers going down. They have stood since the Romans and have not learned to move.

people.source: invented (Rat- + -burg). The ferry, the bridge built about 803-813 and its burning: Einhard 17, 32; Notker I.30; that ferrymen were blamed is a modern retelling (de.wikipedia 'Rheinbrücke Karls des Großen') and is used here only as town talk

people.name: Madalger
people.trait: The king's moneyer at Mainz: slow, exact, proud of his dies and with no patience for a man who argues with a scale.
people.want: Good silver to strike, from anywhere; to see one penny pass in every market before he dies.
people.fear: A light coin found with his mark; his sight going before his son's hand is steady.
people.voice: Short flat sentences; taps the table once when he has finished speaking.
people.looks: Near fifty, thick-set, cropped grey hair, a scorched leather apron over a good green tunic, burn scars on both forearms and a small folding scale on a cord round his neck.
knows: what old pennies and foreign silver fetch against the new penny
the fine for refusing the king's coin
how to nick and weigh silver, and who on the shore passes bad
where strange silver has been seen on the river

ties.note: the Dorestad moneyer and he compare weights by letter and by skipper; each trusts the other's word on a coin
his sister's daughter; he pays her score for the mint's men and checks it
strikes for the king, but under the bishop's eye
the bishop's clerk for the mint at Colonia weighs Mogontia's pennies and writes to say what he found; Madalger weighs Colonia's

lines.greet: Put it on the cloth. All of it. I do not bite coins. I weigh them, which is worse.
lines.greet_again: Your silver was good last time. I remember silver better than faces.
rumour: The king wants one penny in every market from here to the sea, heavier than the old. Good. A penny should not need an argument.
Men bring me old pennies and ask if they are still money. They are still silver. That is not the same thing.
lines.law: The new penny is to be taken everywhere. A free man who refuses it pays fifteen shillings. I did not make the rule. I make the penny.
lines.dirham: This writing is not ours and not the Greeks'. But the scale likes it. Where there is one there are a thousand. Find me the road.
lines.saying: A moneyer's hand belongs to the king. If the coin is false, the king takes it back at the wrist.
lines.farewell: Go well. Bring me anything round and white. I will tell you what it is, and then what it is worth.

people.source: invented (Madal- + -ger). The Mainz penny of 771-794: Münzkabinett Berlin 18245022. The new penny and the fine of fifteen shillings: synod of Frankfurt 794, c. 5 (chronicle_793.json 794-06-frankfurt-new-denier). The loss of the hand for false coin is later Carolingian law (?)

people.name: Brunric
people.trait: Given as a hostage at thirteen and kept twenty years in a bishop's household among the Alemans: careful, courteous, and no longer sure whose man he is.
people.want: To know whether his mother lives, and to be asked, once, what he himself wants.
people.fear: Being sent home to a place that is gone; being kept from a wife who is not on any list.
people.voice: Speaks Frankish the southern way and Saxon like a boy of thirteen, slowly, hunting for the words.
people.looks: Thirty-three, tall and fair like his brother but thinner, hair cut short in the Frankish way, shaven chin, a scar through the left eyebrow, a vine-dresser's hooked knife at his belt.
knows: the bishops' and counts' households on the upper Rhine and the lake
how vines are pruned and wine is kept
which of the thirty-seven mean to run
what a hostage hears at a lord's table in twenty years

ties.note: his elder brother, the mate, who has asked for him along the whole river
the same brother, in his home port
his mother; she asks every boat about a boy with a split eyebrow
the clerk asked him how his name is said and wrote it so
has heard that a priest who speaks Saxon is made teacher of his people; would like to believe it
given as a hostage in the same year from the same river; they were children on the same road south

lines.greet: You speak slowly for me. Good. I have not had Saxon in my mouth since I was thirteen. It tastes of milk.
lines.greet_again: You came back. In twenty years nobody has come back for me. I do not yet know what to do with it.
rumour: They count us at mid-Lent. Some are to go home, they say. Nobody says which. A hostage learns not to ask.
My keeper's vines stand on a south slope above a lake. I have pruned them fourteen winters. A man grows fond of what he prunes.
lines.mother: Is she alive? Tell me that first. Then tell me whether Brunger still chews his moustache when he is angry.
lines.choice: I have a wife who has never seen the Weser and a brother who has never seen my wife. Whichever boat I take, I leave kin on a bank.
lines.saying: A hostage is a debt somebody else owes. I have been owed for twenty years.
lines.farewell: If I am not in your boat, give her this lock of hair. Tell her the eyebrow healed crooked. She will know.

people.source: invented; the name, the age and the scar are those of places/daventre.json (daventre.the_counted_son). The hostages brought to Mainz at mid-Lent about 805: Indiculus obsidum Saxonum Moguntiam deducendorum, MGH Capitularia I no. 115 (?). His death year is unknown to the game (0): it hangs on the story's ending

people.name: Gundhart
people.trait: A grain man of the town with two boats of his own on the Main: big, slow-spoken, generous with a lift and hard about a measure.
people.want: Mills that grind and hulls that carry; to be the man the bishop sends for when bread is short.
people.fear: A wet harvest upriver; being taken for one of the dealers who sell after dark.
people.voice: Talks of the Main as of a difficult ox; counts in sacks, never in pennies, until the bargain is struck.
people.looks: About forty, tall and thick in the middle, brown beard, a floury grey tunic under a good brown cloak with a round bronze brooch, a notched measuring stick in his fist.
knows: what wheat, rye and barley cost from the upper Main to the Rhine mouth
the king's top price and his own lower one, and who breaks them
which mills need stones and which abbeys need bread
who has taken passage on the grain boats, and where to

ties.note: takes the Colonia stone dealer's millstones up to the mills on the Main and brings him flour-money back
the king's steward at Deutz is always short of hulls; Gundhart has lent him one more than once
says a Frisian sells what makes men foolish and he sells what keeps them alive
first name on the clerk's list of hulls, and means to stay there
his boatmen's score at her house, settled each Martinmas in barley for her brewing
the count's steward at Dorestad measures his sacks with a larger measure than he sells by
the king's steward at the Ruhr mouth buys his oats and rye for the hostage bands and pays on the day, which Gundhart says of no other officer on the river

lines.greet: A sea boat, this far up. Well. What do you want carried, or what will you carry?
lines.greet_again: You are back with the high water. Good. I have forty sacks for the lower river and one boat too few.
rumour: Upriver the ears stood full and empty both, last harvest. Men rubbed them and got dust. I buy by weight now, not by the look.
The king has set the price of wheat and set his own lower. I sell at his. There are men on this shore who do not.
lines.passage: I take pilgrims down the Main for nothing when the boat is light. A blind man once. It costs me a seat and God keeps the tally.
lines.warm: When the bishop's clerk asks me who else is honest with a measure, I shall have a name for him.
lines.saying: Grain is the only cargo that asks to be let out. Keep it dry or it will leave by itself.
lines.farewell: Go down gently, and tell Meginher at Colonia the upper mill wants two stones before the harvest.

people.source: invented (Gund- + -hart); the id is the one places/colonia.json ties to. Mainz grain merchants who bought in the upper parts of Germany, boated grain down the Main and gave a blind man passage: Einhard, Translation of SS. Marcellinus and Peter (tr. Wendell 1926), for about 830; set a generation earlier here. The false grain of 792-793: spine.json hungry_years. The top prices: Frankfurt 794

people.name: Hrabanus
people.trait: The most learned man in the kingdom, born in this city, schooled at Fulda and Tours: grave, tireless, and practical about bread.
people.want: Grain for the poor in the hungry years; quiet in which to write; an end to preachers who frighten people for gain.
people.fear: False teaching spreading faster than he can answer it; the poor dying at his gate.
people.voice: Slow and exact, an old teacher's habit of asking a question he already knows the answer to.
people.looks: Near seventy, tall and stooped, a bald crown and white fringe, a plain black monk's habit under a bishop's cloak, ink on the right forefinger, a small book always in the left hand.
knows: what grain costs from the Main to the sea in a famine year
the councils' rulings and why
every book worth copying and which house holds it
the story of Saint Alban, which he wrote down himself

ties.note: Alcuin taught him at Tours and gave him the name Maurus; he speaks of him as of a father
a fellow bishop of the eastern kingdom; the mission to the Danes is discussed at his councils
a Dane holding Dorestad from the emperor is, to him, a wolf set to keep the fold
sends books and good advice to the priest among the Frisians
has the chair after Otgar, who stood with the emperor Lothar against the eastern king; Hrabanus stood with Lothar too, and paid for it with his abbey (?)

lines.greet: I was born inside these walls. I went away to learn and came back to be asked for bread. Sit. What does grain cost downriver?
lines.greet_again: The merchant who answers plainly. I have forty clerks and could use one of you.
rumour: A woman called Thiota told this city the world would end within the year. Men gave her gifts. A priest had taught her the words, for his share.
The monk Gottschalk says God chose the lost before they were born. We condemned it here. He has not stopped saying it.
lines.hunger: At Winkel I feed three hundred a day and it is not enough. Bring grain and name an honest price. I will remember both.
lines.warm: I will have your house written in the book we read from at the altar. It is a longer reckoning than the count's, and kinder.
lines.saying: A full barn in a hungry year is a sermon against its owner.
lines.farewell: Go with God. If you meet Fulda's men on the Main, tell them their old abbot still wakes for the night office.

people.source: Annales Fuldenses 847, 848, 850 (Thiota, Gottschalk, the famine and Winkel); de.wikipedia 'Rabanus Maurus': born at Mainz about 780, abbot of Fulda, archbishop 847-856. Alcuin's pupil at Tours and the byname Maurus: from memory (?). The oldest account of Saint Alban is in his martyrology (en.wikipedia 'Alban of Mainz'). His words are invented

people.name: Liutefred
people.trait: A rich merchant of the city whom the king trusted with an embassy to the Greeks: shrewd, travelled, a little too fond of telling it.
people.want: Hulls to carry spice and silk downriver, and listeners.
people.fear: That a younger house will learn the road over the mountains; that the king will send him again.
people.voice: Easy and worldly; drops a Greek word and then explains it.
people.looks: About fifty, stout, a trimmed dark beard going grey, a long red wool gown with a strip of patterned silk at the neck, a gold ring, a purse of soft foreign leather.
knows: the road from Mainz over the Alps to Venice and the sea-road beyond
what pepper, silk and cloves cost at each step
how the Greek court receives envoys and their gifts
which spice men by the gate weigh fair

ties.note: the bishop of Traiectum buys his silk for the altar and his pepper for the table
the king's brother, archbishop at Colonia from 953, is the one man on the river who answers his Greek words in Greek (?); Liutefred has stopped using them there

lines.greet: A river man. Good. I have been where rivers are not enough. Sit, and I will try not to talk of it all evening.
lines.greet_again: You again. Then you want pepper or stories. Pepper I sell. The stories I cannot stop.
rumour: I left Venice the day after Saint Bartholomew's and saw the Greeks' city three weeks and two days later, with the king's letters in my shirt.
The envoy who sailed with me had a letter from his lord and no gifts. He gave his own and named them his master's. I said nothing.
lines.trade: Spice comes over the mountains in a saddlebag and goes down this river in a cask. You have the casks. Shall we talk?
lines.warm: Take my token to the spice men by the gate. They will show you silver with no king's face, and weigh it fairer than the mint.
lines.saying: At home I am a rich man. In the Greeks' city I was a man with nine good cloaks. It is healthy to learn the difference.
lines.farewell: Go down easily. I envy you a road where every toll man speaks your tongue.

people.source: Liudprand, Antapodosis VI.4-6 (tr. F. A. Wright 1930): 'Liutefred, a rich merchant of Maintz', Otto's envoy, left Venice 25 August 949, reached Constantinople 17 September; Liudprand, who sailed with him, gave his own gifts as his lord's (?). Nothing else is known of him: his years (940-960), his looks and his words are invented, and his birth and death are unknown (0). A tie to the Norwegian Ohthere, who told his voyage at King Alfred's court two generations earlier, was taken out: nothing joins the two

people.name: Otgar
people.trait: Archbishop in the emperor Louis's years: a great man's kinsman grown into a great man, hospitable, political, sure that the right emperor is the eldest son.
people.want: Relics for his churches, the emperor Lothar's cause upheld on the Rhine, and the abbot Einhard's goodwill, which is worth a letter at court.
people.fear: The eastern king across the river with an army and a long memory.
people.voice: Genial and roundabout; says three courteous things and puts the request in the fourth.
people.looks: About fifty in 830, tall and fleshy, a silver-grey tonsure, a deep blue cloak with a border of gold thread, a heavy ring, and white baptismal linen still kept folded in a chest to show guests.
knows: what was promised to the baptised king of the Danes and what he was given
which brother each count and bishop on the Rhine is for, this month
the road of a pack-load of wax from the Scheldt to the Main, since the abbot's men lodge with him on the way
where relics can be had beyond the mountains, and what they cost in gifts

ties.note: the abbot of the two houses at Ganda lives in his province, at Seligenstadt on the Main, and writes to him; Einhard's wax and letters from the Scheldt pass under his wall
Colonia's archbishop gave the Danish king a boat; Otgar gave him baptism, and thinks the annals should say which was the greater gift
saw the young monk set out with the Danish king in 826 and did not expect to hear of either again (?)
the abbot of Fulda is the more learned man and will have his chair after him; they agree about the emperor and about nothing else (?)
finds an old clerk of Riculf's still keeping the lists in 826 and has the sense to leave him at it

lines.greet: A shipman of the lower river. You are welcome; sit. I baptised a king of your northern neighbours on this hill. Tell me, is he still a king?
lines.greet_again: You are back, and with news, I hope, and not only wine. Though the wine is welcome. What do they say at Dorestat of the emperor's sons?
rumour: The king of the Danes went under the water on Saint John's day, and his wife, and more of his people than my clerks could count linen for.
The abbot Einhard reckons fifteen days from Ganda to his house on the Main. His men lodge here on the way. They say twelve, when he is not by.
There are three brothers and one empire. I am for the eldest, as God made him. Say so downriver, or do not; it is known.
lines.trade: Wax, incense and good linen for the church; and if you hear of a saint's body to be had honestly beyond the mountains, tell my clerk before you tell Fulda.
lines.saying: It is easier to baptise a king than to keep him one.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and greet the abbot's steward at Ganda if you pass. Tell him the wax arrived, and how much of it.

people.source: Otgar, archbishop of Mainz 826 to 847 (de.wikipedia 'Otgar von Mainz', by way of the dossier's list). The baptism of Harald with his wife and many Danes on 24 June 826, at Saint Alban's by the Annales Fuldenses, at Ingelheim by others (dossier 5, 8). Einhard's letter to him: Einhardi opera, ed. Teulet II, letter VIII (dossier 9; not opened (?)). That he held with Lothar against Louis the German, and that he is said to have been Riculf's kinsman, are in the same article (checked 7 October 2026); he died on 21 April 847. His birth year is unknown (0); his looks and words are invented. The id is the one places/ganda.json ties to

people.name: Liutbert
people.trait: Archbishop and the eastern king's archchaplain in the Northmen's years: a churchman who mends walls, counts spears and, once, rides out himself.
people.want: The wall whole and the ditch dug before the next fleet; bread and beds for the clergy of Colonia and their saints; boats that will carry word downriver in winter.
people.fear: Smoke at Bingen. A fire inside his own wall, which no ditch keeps out.
people.voice: Short and practical. Says what is needed, who is to bring it, and by which feast.
people.looks: About sixty in 882, lean and weathered, a white tonsure, a plain grey riding cloak over a mail shirt he does not hide, a bishop's ring and mud on his boots.
knows: how far up the river the Northmen have burned, by the day
which houses on the shore have paid their share of the wall and which have not
where the canons of Colonia and Bonn are lodged, and what treasure came with them
what the king's host can and cannot do this year

ties.note: the king's commander on the lower river: Henry holds the Northmen in their fort at Diusburg in the winter of 883 while Liutbert keeps the upper river; they send each other boats, not letters (?)
the army that sat a year at Ganda is the army that burned Colonia; Liutbert has its leavings lodged in his guest houses and has met some of its men at the sword's length
a Frisian of the Ruhr mouth who comes up for wine brings him the count of ships on the lower river, and is paid for it in toll forgiven
held, like every bishop of the eastern kingdom, that a Dane set to guard the river mouths guards them for his cousins

lines.greet: You came up from the lower river? Then tell me first what burns and what stands. Your wine can wait a quarter of an hour.
lines.greet_again: The house that brings a true count. Sit. How many ships below Colonia, and whose?
rumour: Colonia has burned, and Bonn. Their canons are in my guest houses with their saints in chests. We are a city of two cathedrals and one kitchen.
The wall is being mended and a ditch dug outside it. Every house on the shore is asked for carts or silver. The Frisians gave silver. It was quicker.
I met them on the river with a few men and took back what they carried. Do not make a song of it. They were tired and we were not.
lines.trade: Lime, oak, iron bars for the gates, and grain. I pay in pennies and in toll forgiven. Do not offer me wine; of cellars we are not short.
lines.saying: A wall is prayed for on the inside and paid for on the shore.
lines.farewell: Go down by daylight and come back with the count. If you see smoke at Bingen, do not stop to make sure.

people.source: Liutbert, archbishop of Mainz 863 to 889 and archchaplain (dossier 3). The clergy of Colonia and Bonn at Mainz with their treasures and saints, winter 881/82; the wall mended and a ditch dug, 882; Liutbert with a few men kills many Northmen and takes back the plunder, 883 (Annales Fuldenses 881, 882, 883, ed. Kurze 1891). He and Count Henry fell on a camp of the Northmen together early in 885 (Annales Fuldenses 885, by en.wikipedia 'Henry of Franconia'); their boats and counts in the winter of 883, and his dealings with a Frisian of Diusburg, are invented (?). His birth year is unknown (0); his looks and words are invented. The id is the one places/colonia.json links to

stories.title: Thirty-seven names
stories.summary: About 805 the Saxon hostages kept among the Alemans are ordered brought to Mogontia at mid-Lent to be counted, and one name on the clerk's list is Brunric, the lost brother of Brunger the mate. He is a grown man with a Frankish haircut, a keeper, a wife on no list, and a choice nobody has offered him in twenty years.
stories.picture: The bishop's hall at mid-Lent, grey light: a row of men in borrowed cloaks standing before a clerk's table, one with a scar through his eyebrow turning his head toward a big fair man in the doorway.

beats.text: Hathugard asks every boat about a boy of thirteen with a scar through the left eyebrow. The ferryman knows which lord's men took the boys (the trail: sx_brother_trail). This is told in places/daventre.json.

At the Ruhr mouth, where the road from Saxony meets the river, a Saxon woman in the king's kitchen has counted every hostage band since 785. She remembers twelve Weser boys sent south by boat, and one who would not answer to his new name (also sets sx_brother_trail). This is told in places/diusburg.json.

The clerk Hrotbert at Colonia has the roll of 785: a boy from the Weser, given to a lord of the Alemans, sent on by Mogontia. He reads it for a service done, and sends the roll itself up to Otbert when the king orders the counting.

Ratburg has heard the Daventre woman's question from the boats for years. She knows the bishops upriver keep Saxons in their vineyards, and that sooner or later the king has such men counted. She will send word down when he does.

Otbert has the list: thirty-seven names and their keepers, all to stand in the hall at mid-Lent. For a merchant he has marked honest he reads it aloud. The twenty-ninth is a Frankish name his keeper gave him, and after it, in Otbert's hand: called Brunric, of the Weser. Brunger stops breathing.

beats.when: flag.sx_brother_trail and year >= 804 and year < 807 and fast
beats.text: Mid-Lent. The hostages are counted twice. Brunric answers to his name in the Alemans' speech; the brothers stand an arm's length apart and neither knows the other's tongue well enough to begin (sets sx_brother_found).

On the hill, away from the keepers, Brunric says what he has: a wife, vines, a lord who is not unkind. And what he lacks: his mother's voice. The merchant can ask the bishop for leave, hide him in the boat, or carry his word.
Whatever was found is brought down the river to the ale-house at Daventre before Martinmas.

endings.how: The merchant stood well with the bishop, asked in the hall, and stood surety in silver that Brunric would be given back if the king called for him.
endings.text: Riculf writes three lines. Brunric goes down the river in the open, sitting on the mate's bench beside his brother, and his wife follows by cart at the vintage. Nobody may ask for him.
endings.reward: flag sx_brother_found; Brunger is the house's man for life; the Daventre ending 'home' without the king's men; Otbert and Riculf become friendly; a vine-dresser who knows every cellar on the upper Rhine

endings.how: The merchant took him aboard after dark without leave and was gone under the piers before the second count.
endings.text: The list has thirty-six names at the second counting and Otbert sits a long time over the gap. The king's men have a description. Brunric sees the Weser again.
endings.reward: flags sx_brother_found and sx_carried_fugitive; Brunger is the house's man for life; the merchant is wary-listed in the bishop's hall for some years, and Otbert will not read him another list

endings.how: Brunric chose his wife and his vines, and the merchant did not press him.
endings.text: He cuts a lock of his hair with the vine knife and names the slope where he lives, so that a boat may one day find it. Brunger says nothing as far as Colonia.
endings.reward: flag sx_brother_found; the Daventre ending 'word'; from then on a cask of the keeper's wine waits each Martinmas at Folcbald's cellar, at the grower's price

endings.how: The boat did not lie at Mogontia in the years of the counting.
endings.text: The hostages were counted and sent back to their keepers, or home, and the list went into a chest. Otbert remembers a tall Saxon with a split eyebrow. He does not remember where he went.

stories.reward: A crewman bound to the house for life, a friend among the bishop's clerks, and the road to the upper Rhine's cellars; or a brother's word carried home like silver.

stories.title: Born in the furnace
stories.summary: The riddle of the wine cask, had at the salt pans of Herio, points to where the casks come from. On the Frisians' shore Folcbald keeps a leaf a monk once left him for a debt: Aldhelm's verse on a thing born in the furnace that looks like ice. Its answer leads downriver to a dealer at Colonia.
stories.picture: A cellar door under the Roman wall, lamp-lit: a spare Frisian holding a small leaf of parchment at arm's length, a cask on its side between him and a merchant, a wooden tasting cup on the cask head.

beats.text: The salt dealer's leaf is answered: a wine cask. The next leaf waits where the casks come from.
Folcbald hears the answer, nods, and fetches a leaf from behind the oldest cask. He cannot read it; a monk told him what it says. Latin aboard, or a clerk from the hall, makes it out.
Ratburg knows the answer because Folcbald told her in drink. She will sell it for the price of a round for the house. It is the easy way and Folcbald will know it was taken.

The answer is a cup of glass. The man who sells them at Colonia, Liutwin of the wine house, has the last leaf, and it stings the tongue. Gerhild on the next pitch says a clay cup never set anyone a riddle, and that this is in its favour.

endings.how: The merchant answered the glass-cup riddle himself.
endings.text: Folcbald pours from the cask he does not sell and gives the name of the glass dealer at Colonia, with a word to say to him.
endings.reward: give_riddle riddle_aldhelm_80_calix_vitreus solved; the riddle's own reward (a price word for Colonia); Folcbald friendly; the chain goes on to pepper and the fair of Saint-Denis

endings.how: The merchant bought the answer from Ratburg.
endings.text: The chain goes on all the same. Folcbald says nothing, and for a year his best cask stays shut.
endings.reward: the next step of the chain; no price word; Ratburg friendly, Folcbald cool

endings.how: The merchant took the leaf and never answered it.
endings.text: The leaf lies in the chest. Folcbald asks after it each time, a little more drily.
endings.reward: the leaf as a text in the chest (aldhelm_80_calix_vitreus), to be answered in any later year or by an heir

stories.reward: The third link of the salt-to-pepper chain, a price word for glass at Colonia, and the Frisian's own cask.

stories.title: The king's grain
stories.summary: In the hungry years the Main is the road grain comes down, and the king has set a top price on it and a lower one on his own. The bishop's clerk wants hulls to carry estate grain to the towns downriver and pays in grain; a dealer on the shore offers more than the law allows, for delivery after dark. Half a century later Hrabanus asks the same question of the merchant's heir.
stories.picture: Dusk on the gravel shore: Main boats heaped with sacks, a clerk with a wooden measure struck level, and behind a jetty post a man in a good cloak holding up four fingers.

beats.text: Grain boats lie three deep off the Main's mouth. Otbert lists every hull that will carry the king's wheat to Colonia or Dorestad at the king's price (from the summer of 794, three pennies the measure), one sack in ten for the carrier.
The new public measure stands in the hall. A merchant may have his own struck against it and marked (sets hy_new_measure). Most find theirs was small.
A dealer who gives no name offers half as much again over the top price for any wheat landed on his plot after dark. Ratburg, pouring, does not hear him. She hears everything (sold so: hy_sold_dear).

The king's grain, landed at the king's price where the bread is short, is remembered by the church there (sets hy_fed_poor). On the strand at Colonia the steward Wido counts the Mogontia sacks off himself, against Otbert's list, and is loud about it when the count is whole.
A day below Colonia the steward Raginhard buys Gundhart's oats and rye for the hostage bands that come down the Hellweg. He pays on the day and at the king's price, and asks no boat to wait for him.
Wheat stands at ten pieces of silver the measure. Hrabanus feeds three hundred a day at Winkel, half a day down the river, and asks the house that once carried the king's grain to carry his.

endings.how: The merchant carried the king's grain at the king's price and sold none of it dear.
endings.text: The clerk's mark goes beside the house's name. The bishop hears of it; the towns downriver ate. In 850 Hrabanus's man knows the name before it is said.
endings.reward: flag hy_fed_poor; a sack in ten as carrier's share; standing with the church at Mogontia and Colonia; the unlock mogontia.bishops_carrier

endings.how: The merchant landed wheat on the dealer's plot by night.
endings.text: The silver is heavy and real. Ratburg heard, the count's men may hear, and Otbert moves a name down a list without a word.
endings.reward: silver, half as much again as the top price; flag hy_sold_dear; Otbert cool

endings.how: The merchant named the dealer to the bishop's clerk.
endings.text: The dealer's plot is searched and his grain sold at the king's price from the hall door. The shore knows who told. The Frisians say nothing, and sell the merchant nothing for a season.
endings.reward: the bishop's favour and a tenth of the grain seized; Folcbald and the shore cool for a year

stories.reward: The bishop's carrying in hungry years, across two generations; or quick silver and a name moved down the list.

stories.title: The beast with sixty teeth
stories.summary: Riculf has an ivory comb for his old master Alcuin and a list of books the school at Saint Alban's lacks. Whoever carries the comb down the Rhine and round to the Loire dry and whole brings back Alcuin's thanks, which is a riddle, and the right to carry copies between the schools of Mogontia, Traiectum and York.
stories.picture: A bishop's lean hands holding out a small ivory comb with two carved beasts' heads on its back, over a table of open books; a merchant's rope-scarred hands not yet daring to take it.

beats.text: Riculf shows the comb: elephant's tooth, two heads carved on the back, thirty teeth a side. It is for Alcuin at Tours, with a letter. He asks who sails toward the Loire, and how dry their hold is.

Otbert adds his own errand: the school wants Bede on the reckoning of time, and has an Aldhelm to lend to Traiectum in return. He teaches what a book is worth and how it is wrapped (sets bk_knows_worth).

Going down, the comb lies a night at Colonia. Bishop Hildebold asks to see what Mogontia is sending his old master, turns it over once, and says that Riculf always did give presents with teeth in them. He adds a letter of his own to the packet.

A boat bound for the Loire by the Scheldt mouth lies at Ganda, and Einold the book-keeper, who copies every letter of Alcuin's that passes, begs a sight of the answer on its way back. He has the riddle by heart before the wax is cold.
Radger the schoolmaster takes the Aldhelm on loan and sends a leaf-count of what he has from York. He will not say which house got the better book.
At the Loire's mouth a monk of Saint Martin's of Tours is waiting for salt and takes the comb and the letter upriver. Before the boat sails again he is back with the answer.
Riculf reads Alcuin's thanks aloud and laughs: a beast with two heads and sixty teeth, and not as big as an elephant. He has the merchant's name written among the church's carriers (sets bk_carried).

endings.how: The comb reached Alcuin's man whole and the answer came back.
endings.text: The riddle is told at the bishop's table for a month and the merchant with it. The school orders calfskin and wax by the year.
endings.reward: flags bk_carried and bk_parchment; Alcuin's comb riddle told to the house (a text for the chest, if the spine adds it); Riculf a fast friend; three lines to Hildebold at Colonia

endings.how: The comb came to harm on the way, and the merchant came back and said so.
endings.text: Riculf counts the teeth that are left and sends it on anyway, with a second letter making a joke of it. Otbert makes a different mark by the name.
endings.reward: the truth told is remembered: Riculf stays easy; no standing order; the books still go by the house's boat, at the house's risk

endings.how: The merchant sold the ivory in a northern market.
endings.text: It fetches a good price from a man who thinks it a toy. The bishop hears by Martinmas. No clerk on the Rhine will put a book in the house's hold for a generation.
endings.reward: silver, about a pound; flag bk_lost; the church's standing lost at Mogontia and Traiectum

stories.reward: A riddle from Alcuin's own hand, a standing order from the school, and a bishop who writes three lines when they are needed.

stories.title: Three hours in May
stories.summary: For ten years the king's bridge creeps out over the old piers toward the ferrymen's trade, and in May 813, hardly finished, it burns to the water in three hours. Some call it an accident; some say rascals fired it to rob the boats that passed beneath; the shore says ferrymen. Ratburg's brother poles the ferry, and the merchant was in harbour that night.
stories.picture: Night on the river: a line of fire five hundred paces long reflected in black water, the stone piers showing dark beneath it, small boats pulling clear and a woman on the shore holding a man back by the belt.

beats.text: The king's carpenters are laying oak on the old piers. The ferrymen watch from the bank. Ratburg's brother says a bridge is a ferry that does not need feeding, and spits.

The bridge is all but across, and in the spring of 813 it stands. Carts cross in the time a ferry takes to load. Boats pass beneath, and now and then a bale goes missing between one pier and the next; nobody sees how.

The bridge burned in three hours and nothing is left above the water. The bishop's men are asking who was on the river that night. Ratburg asks the merchant what he saw from his boat, and what he will say he saw.

The barge men have the story at the ale-house in the tower at Colonia within the week, in Ratburg's telling and in two others. Adaltrud says a town with only stumps of a bridge, like hers, has at least nothing left to burn, and asks which telling the bishop's hall will write down.
Witnesses are heard in the hall. The king, it is said, means to build again in stone. He is old, and it is said quietly.

endings.how: The merchant swore to what he saw: a fire that began in the middle, with no boat near.
endings.text: The hall writes it down as mischance, as the king's own biographer will. The ferry has its trade again and the ferrymen do not forget whose oath it was.
endings.reward: Ratburg a fast friend; free crossing and a free pilot through the piers for the house, in this generation and the next

endings.how: The merchant said he was asleep.
endings.text: Nothing is proved. The shore goes on saying ferrymen, the ferrymen go on saying rascals, and the piers stand bare.
endings.reward: Nothing gained or lost; Ratburg remembers who would not stand up

endings.how: The merchant named the men he had seen working the boats under the bridge by night.
endings.text: Two river thieves are taken and one bale-hook is shown in the hall. Whether they lit the fire nobody learns. The grain men thank him; the back lanes of the shore do not.
endings.reward: the bishop's thanks and a share of goods recovered; a safer shore for cargo left by night; an enemy among the river thieves

stories.reward: The ferrymen's friendship and a free pilot under the piers, or the bishop's thanks; and either way a seat at the telling for fifty years.

works.name: A jetty on the Frisians' shore
works.what: A plank jetty on oak posts at the foot of a long narrow plot, so that a boat lies afloat and loads from a barrow instead of from men's shoulders in the shallows.
works.needs: A plot on the shore (unlock_plot_mogontia), and oak from the Main rafts.
works.gives: Loading and unloading here takes half the time and no porters; the boat need not be dragged up the gravel; a second hull may lie alongside.
works.picture: A new plank jetty running out from a narrow fenced plot, a river boat tied to it, the Roman wall behind and a carpenter driving the last post from a raft.
works.source: Landesmuseum Mainz, Aurea Magontia, 'From near and far': plots from the wall to the river, each with its jetty. The cost is the game's

works.name: A cellar under the wall
works.what: A vault at the foot of the Roman wall cleared, floored with rails and given a door and a lock, to hold wine bought at the vintage until the price turns.
works.needs: Folcbald's good word, or a plot of your own; the bishop's leave, since the wall is his to keep.
works.gives: Up to forty casks may be bought at the vintage price and kept here; wine stored in it does not spoil in the summer heat.
works.picture: A low stone vault with a new oak door standing open, casks being rolled in on rails by lamplight, a chalk tally fresh on the post.
works.source: The vintage and Martinmas wine: Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md. Roman vaults used as cellars are a guess (?)

works.name: Stone for Saint Alban's
works.what: A boatload of dressed stone, lime and roofing lead given to Riculf's great church on the hill, where the queen lies and the archbishops will.
works.needs: An audience with Riculf, and a hull to bring the stone from the quarries downriver.
works.gives: The house is named among the church's benefactors and prayed for on Saint Alban's day; standing with the church here; a grave on the hill for the merchant, if he wants one.
works.picture: Ox-carts hauling pale stone up a hill road between old graves, the half-built aisles of a great church above, a bishop with lime on his hem pointing where it is to go.
works.source: de.wikipedia 'Stift St. Alban vor Mainz': built under Riculf, consecrated 1 December 805. Lay gifts of stone are a guess

works.name: A share in the wall and the ditch
works.what: The Northmen have burned as far as Koblenz. The old wall is being mended and a ditch dug outside it: every house that trades here is asked for men, carts or silver.
works.needs: Asked for by the archbishop's men in the hall; refusing costs standing.
works.gives: Goods and the boat may be brought inside the wall on any alarm; the archbishop's toll is halved for the house for ten years.
works.picture: Men with baskets of earth on a raw ditch-bank under a patched Roman wall, new pale mortar between old grey stones, a clerk counting carts.
works.source: Annales Fuldenses 882: the wall of Mainz repaired and a ditch dug. The toll remission is the game's

works.name: Bronze for the bishop's doors
works.what: Willigis is building a cathedral east of Saint Martin's, and Master Berenger is to cast its doors: the first of metal since Charles's. It burns on its consecration day in 1009 and is begun again; copper and tin are wanted either way.
works.needs: Copper and tin brought up the river, or silver in their place; an audience with the archbishop.
works.gives: The house's mark is set where the casting was paid for; high standing with the archbishop, who is the king's chancellor; a place at the consecration of 1036 for the heir.
works.picture: A casting pit in a builders' yard, a tall bronze door-leaf lying in its mould with men ladling metal, the unfinished red sandstone of a cathedral behind.
works.source: de.wikipedia 'Mainzer Dom': Willigis's cathedral, burned 29/30 August 1009, consecrated 10 November 1036; the bronze doors of Master Berenger, 'the first metal doors since Charles'. The year building began (about 990) is a guess (?)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The boat of this reach: flat-bottomed, plank-built, with a short mast forward for the tow line. She drifts down laden with casks and is hauled home on the rope. Oak comes down the Main in rafts to the bank where she is built.
ships.picture: A flat barge half-planked on trestles on a gravel bank, a short mast stepped well forward, a Roman wall behind.
ships.source: Design/content/ships.md 4 (the Krefeld-Gellep barge, 8th century, 15.2 m, mast step read as a towing mast); Wandalbert, Miracula sancti Goaris: hauled by rope from the bank 'as the custom is'

ships.note: Frisian shippers bring these up from the delta and sell an old one sooner than haul her home empty in a bad year.
ships.picture: A long hollowed-oak freighter with a raised plank a side, nosed on the shore, a Frisian chalking a price on her bow.
ships.source: Design/content/ships.md (the Utrecht type; Vleuten 1); that they changed hands at Mainz is a guess

ships.note: The archbishop's own river ship, lent with her crew to a house that carries for the church: for a bishop's journey to an assembly, or his wine to the palace.
ships.picture: A long river ship with an awning aft and eight oarsmen, a cross on a pole at her stem, lying off the river gate.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json river_estate_ship; the king himself came down the Main by boat at Christmas 793 (chronicle_793.json)

ships.note: The Kastel ferrymen sell an old barge when a new one is built. In the ten years the king's bridge is building, 803 to 813, they sell cheap.
ships.picture: A broad flat ferry with a horse and a cart aboard, poled across brown water past a stone pier.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json ferry_barge; the crossing by boat: Einhard 17, 32 (dossier 1)

ships.how: bought to break up or to ride down
ships.note: Timber rafts come down the Main and are sold here as oak. A merchant may buy one whole, load it and ride it to the delta, where it is sold again as wood.
ships.picture: A raft of long oak logs lashed with withies, a hut of bark on it and two men with sweeps, coming out of the Main's mouth.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json raft; Design/content/ships.md. Main rafting in this period is a guess (?)

ships.note: Every plot on the shore has an errand boat; a leaky one costs a few pennies.
ships.picture: A small flat skiff tied under a jetty, a boy bailing it with a wooden scoop.

sayings.text: What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed and when I am on horseback I cannot shield myself with them against wind and rain.
sayings.source: Notker, Deeds of Charles I.34 (tr. A. J. Grant 1905): the king on the Frisians' short cloaks, sold at the long price

sayings.text: The bridge burned by the knavery of a few rascals, who wanted to steal merchandise from the ships that passed underneath.
sayings.source: Notker, Deeds of Charles I.30 (tr. A. J. Grant 1905), lightly joined; Einhard calls it an accident

sayings.text: So completely consumed in three hours by an accidental fire that not a single splinter of it was left, except what was under water.
sayings.source: Einhard, Life of Charles 32 (tr. S. E. Turner 1880), checked against the text at sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/einhard.asp

sayings.text: The pots knocked together and broke, as the potters said.
A very large city, part of it lived in and the rest sown.
sayings.source: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub in al-Qazwini, after G. Jacob's German (1896), our English; said of Mainz in 965

sayings.text: What beast has two heads and sixty teeth and is not as big as an elephant? A comb.
sayings.source: after Alcuin's letter of thanks to Riculf, about 796; a paraphrase, not a translation (Things That Talk, after Sorrell)

sayings.text: Down is free. Up is paid for at every step.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: the haulers' word for the river

sayings.text: New wine by Martinmas, new quarrels by Advent.
A Frisian measures his cloak short and his memory long.
Pray at Saint Goar's going up. The rocks are still there coming down.
sayings.source: invented, after Wandalbert, Miracula sancti Goaris (about 839)

sayings.text: Why does a ferryman love a flood? It is the only bridge-builder that works for him.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: a riddle-joke of the shore

sayings.text: A wall this long was built by men who expected company.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: said of the Roman wall and the gardens inside it

easter_eggs.text: The game begins on 21 June 793. At Mogontia that is Saint Alban's day: a boat that could be here on its first morning would find the hill full of pilgrims. No boat from Dorestad can.

Under the gravel of the Frisians' shore lie five Roman warships, sunk in the mud four hundred years before. A man digging a jetty post strikes old oak and curses it. Nobody will know what it is for another twelve hundred years.
The potters' row is the first place in the town to know of an earthquake: before cockcrow at the turn of 881 their pots knocked together on the shelves and broke.

The woman Thiota foretold the last day for 847, and people brought her gifts as to a saint. Before the bishops she said a priest had taught her the words, for gain. An old hauler at the ale-house still has the cheese-press he did not give her.
easter_eggs.source: Annales Fuldenses 847; the hauler is invented

easter_eggs.text: In 873 locusts a thumb long came from the east, lay on the fields like snow and ate a hundred iugera near the town in an hour. The annalist counted their teeth as harder than stone.
easter_eggs.source: Annales Fuldenses 873; the teeth are from memory of the same entry (?)

easter_eggs.text: In 965 a stranger from Tortosa stands a long time at a spice stall, turning over silver struck at Samarkand fifty years before, and asks in bad Frankish how pepper comes to grow so far west. He writes something down in letters that run the wrong way.
easter_eggs.source: G. Jacob 1896, pp. 37-38 (Ibrahim ibn Yaqub in al-Qazwini)

easter_eggs.text: About the year 1000 the head of the Jews' school rules that no man may read a letter meant for another. A merchant who carries letters hears of it from the spice men, and is told it is a good rule for Christians too.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia 'Gershom ben Judah' (rulings of about 1000); no Jews are attested at Mainz before the 10th century (dossier 8)

easter_eggs.text: Archbishop Erkanbald, who dies in 1021, is laid in his coffin the wrong way round, in blue silk with a gold border. He was a tall man, and gouty. Nobody says why he was turned.
easter_eggs.source: de.wikipedia 'Erkanbald' (the coffin opened in 2019: 1.82 m tall)

easter_eggs.text: The round tower by Saint Alban's road has no door because it is a grave: a Roman general's, the stonecutters say, though none can say which. Boys dare each other to climb it at midsummer.
easter_eggs.source: de.wikipedia 'Drususstein'; what people of 793 called it is unknown (?)

easter_eggs.text: Queen Fastrada is carried up the hill in August 794. A clerk says the king chose Saint Alban's himself, over the abbeys where queens lie; the masons work round the grave for eleven more years.
easter_eggs.source: Annales Fuldenses 794; de.wikipedia 'Stift St. Alban vor Mainz'. The clerk's word is invented

easter_eggs.text: On Saint John's day 826 the shore fills with Danes in new white baptismal linen: King Harald's people, baptised with him. The poet at court says they came up the river in a hundred white-sailed ships; the haulers who watched say fewer, and that Danes do not tip.
easter_eggs.source: Annales Fuldenses 826; Ermoldus Nigellus, In honorem Hludowici IV (?) for the white sails; Mainz or Ingelheim is disputed (dossier 8). The haulers are invented

easter_eggs.text: Willigis's pennies show his own head. An old moneyer's grandson at the mint turns one over twice to be sure there is still a king on the other side.
easter_eggs.source: Landesmuseum Mainz, Aurea Magontia, 'Archbishop Willigis': the first archbishop in the kingdom with his own head on a coin. The grandson is invented
